content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper studies the problem of causal representation learning, where the goal is to recover the latent variables from a set of observations. The authors attempt to study settings where the assumption of injectivity no longer holds and to do so propose a hierarchy of generative functions that include a notion of occlusion.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: 

* The paper tackles a very important problem within representation learning, i.e., what can we do with non-injective functions?
* The authors do a good job of delivering the main ideas of their work. The paper was easy to follow.


Weaknesses:

* I believe the main weakness is that I don't consider this work to be complete in the sense that the main technical results are incremental results from Ahuja et al.. Moreover, there is not a single synthetic experiment to give more understanding of the results. Then, the work does not shine either in technical or experimental contributions. I believe the idea of studying settings with non-injective functions is great, but the set of contributions of this work in its current shape is not enough for publication at ICLR.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity is great, most of the points are clear.

Quality: The work lacks more technical contributions and experiments.

Novelty: I think the novelty is in studying a new setting, but more contributions are required.

Reproducibility: No experiments are provided.
content.summary_of_the_review: As I said above, the paper studies a very important setting. However, in my opinion, more contributions are needed for publication.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the topic of causal (unsupervised) representation learning.  There are the following two main contributions. The authors first introduce a concept of the hierarchy of representation learning systems from the observational view. Then, the authors demonstrate that one can relax the injective assumption and achieve some identifiability results.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength

The concept of the hierarchy of representation learning systems is novel and the non-injective identification results are non-trivial. 

The analysis is presented in a logical way.

Weakness

The identification results only focus on some special models. 

Some concerns or questions 

1. Regarding Level 3: as the authors said, the model follows the nonlinear ICA, thus the elements in $z$ are independent of each other. If It is, in your Level 3, there exists some latent that may not have the observations and affect the latent $z$. This will imply that the elements in $z$ may not be independent of each other.  Graphically speaking, the graph of Level 3 will be a latent hierarchical structure where some latent variables may not have directly observed variables but have unobserved variables as children.  The authors may need to point out the difference between standard ICA and the setting of Level 3.

2. Regarding Level 4: I totally agree that the problem of level 4 is interesting. However, I can not sure if it is necessary to introduce it in the observation hierarchy. I can not imagine the role of latent $U$ in the underlying causal graph.  Can you explain more about the connection between this level and Peral's causal hierarchy?


minor typos

Page 6: Level 4: Unconstrained latents---> miss 2.4 

The paragraph of "beyond known mechanisms" on Page 9: would have have recovered identification up to--->double have?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
This paper is well-written.

The idea of four levels is new.  The authors proposed some illustrations to explain them.
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed hierarchy concept is interesting. It makes some progress on the hard problem of learning the causal representation under the non-injection assumption.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
In the context of causal representation learning, the paper proposes four hierarchical levels of non-injectivity in the generator $g: Z \to X$, mapping from latent variables to observed variables. (1) the generator is injective; (2) there are multiple viewpoints and a combination of viewpoints is injective; (3) no viewpoints disambiguate different latent values, but there is some SCM structure on the latent space and some ability to do interventions, which affect the distribution on $X$ for different values of the latent; (4) there is no such intervention. 

The authors extend prior work on identifiability when the latent mechanism is known, to the non-injective setting. Their extension states that when the latent is restricted to a subset of latent on which the generator is injective, identifiability with a known latent mechanism is possible.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strength
I think it's great that the authors study partial observability in causal representation learning. This is certainly a next step in the field.

### Weaknesses
On the proposed hierarchy:
- In level 2 in sec 2, it seems like having different viewpoints can just as well be interpreted as a combined map $Z \to \prod_{v \in V}X : z \mapsto (g(z, v))_v$ and requiring that this map is injective. It seems like level 2 that way trivially maps back to level 1. It there therefore much value in making the discrimination between levels 1 and 2?
- The authors propose a distinction between levels 3 and 4, but give no theory to show that identifiability is possible in some cases in level 3, but not in 4. I thus don't see the value of making the distinction between level 3 and 4 in this paper.
- Levels 1 and 2 make no statement about the generating processes on $Z$, only on the generator function $g$, while levels 3 and 4 require an SCM on $Z$ to be specified. The proposed hierarchy therefore doesn't really appear like a hierarchy and more like a collection of different regimes.

On the proposed identifiability:
- The identifiability result in level 2 is only developed in the limited regime in which the mechanism in latent space is known, the regime studied in the work by Ahuja et al (2022). When the mechanism is not known, the identifiability is only up to a (possibly large) equivalence class. This significant limitation should be made clearly in the abstract.
- The identifiability result in Theorem 2, extends the prior work by Ahuja et al, deriving (partial) identifiability in the subset of latents for which the generator is injective. That would be a very limited extension.
- It seems like the setup in section 3.2 "Level 2 identification", Theorem 2, doesn't satisfy the definition of "Level 2" in definition 2. In Theorem 2, what is the set of viewpoints that make the generator injective?


Additionally, there are no experiments and I think the theory is not substantial enough to warrant that.


Minor points:
- The authors write "To develop identification results, first we establish that just before and after the non-injective time points, the observations are injective, and the corresponding latent variables are identified up to some transformation at these points." Is this a general result? If so, the authors should prove it. Or is it an assumption on the situations considered? If so, the authors should be more clear about it.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
### Clarity
the paper is mostly easy to follow. However section 3.2 relies too heavily on the prior work by Ahuja et al (2019) and is difficult to read stand-alone.

Small suggestion: the claims in the paper mostly works on the level of sets (the category of sets). In that context, right/left invertibility are equivalent to surjectivity and injectivity. Perhaps the authors could use those more intuitive terms in section 3.1 and appendix A.

### Quality
The claims seem well-supported.

### Novelty
Insufficient

### Reproducibility
Not applicable
content.summary_of_the_review: I'm not quite convinced about the novelty nor the usefulness of the proposed hierarchy. The identifiability results are a very marginal extension of prior work. The theoretical contribution is thus limited. Combined with the lack of experiments, I don't think this is sufficient for publication.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper defines a causal hierarchy for causal representation learning, which relaxes the common assumption of injectivity of the function that maps from the latent causal variables to the observations. More precisely, the paper proposes a hierarchy in which the first level contains injective functions and the fourth (and last) one contains variables that are not contained by the observations. In addition to introducing this hierarchy, the paper's main result is an identifiability theorem that applies to non-injective mappings, which is arguably the first such result for the non-injective case.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The hierarchy presented in the paper is a relevant contribution to strengthening and widening the formal framework that supports causal representation learning. The paper is written in a very clear and precise way. 

On the other hand, arguably, the paper falls short of showing the usefulness of the proposed hierarchy, in that the paper does not include any concrete instantiation of the abstract formalism therein introduced.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is technically solid, with high quality, and written in a very clear and readable way. The work is, to the best of my knowledge, original and relevant, although one may argue that it is not highly innovative, since the proposed extension of the hierarchy is quite natural and comes across as a natural choice to extend the framework beyond injectivity.
 
There is something wrong in the statement of Definition 3: it starts by defining a latent variable U, but then this variable is never again mentioned in the definition.
content.summary_of_the_review: A good and solid paper, in some sense, a paper of foundational nature, but which would gain from further instantiation of at least some of the levels of the proposed hierarchy.

content.title: Beyond the injective assumption in causal representation learning
content.TL;DR: A hierarchy of generative functions for causal representation learning to consider that relaxes the injective assumption.
content.abstract: Causal representation learning aims to take some entangled observation, $x$, and recover the latent causal variables $z$ from which the observation was generated using via generative function $g(\cdot): \mathcal{Z}\rightarrow \mathcal{X}$. While this problem is impossible in its full generality, there has been considerable recent progress in showing a variety of conditions in which the latents are identifiable. All of these approaches share the assumption that $g(\cdot)$ is injective: i.e. for any two observations $x_1$ and $x_2$, if $x_1 = x_2$ then the corresponding latent variables, $z_1$ and $z_2$ are equal. This assumption is restrictive but dropping it entirely would allow pathological examples that we could never hope to identify, so in order to make progress beyond injectivity, we need to make explicit the important classes of non-injective functions. In this paper we present formal hierarchy over generative functions that includes injective functions and two non-trivial classes of non-injective functions---occlusion and observable effects---that we argue are important for causal representation learning to consider. We demonstrate that the injective assumption is not necessary, by proving the first identifiability results in settings with occluded variables.
